summary: After John the Baptist is imprisoned, Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, preaching that the kingdom of God is at hand.
key_insight: Herod Antipas had just put John in prison, and Herod ruled Galilee. Jesus did not go quiet. He walked into Herod’s territory and took up John’s call to repent, with news John could only point toward: the time is fulfilled.
story: Jesus heard that John had been put in prison. {Mt} After His two days among the Samaritans, He went on to Galilee, {Jn} and He returned in the power of the Spirit. {Lk}

Jesus Himself had said that a prophet has no honor in his own country. When He came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed Him. Many of them had gone up to Jerusalem for the feast and had seen all the things He did there. {Jn}
He came preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand. Repent, and believe in the gospel.” {Mk}
He taught in their synagogues and was glorified by all, and news of Him went out through all the surrounding region. {Lk}
differences: Matthew and Mark connect Jesus’ return to Galilee with John’s imprisonment. John connects His leaving Judea with the Pharisees hearing that He was making more disciples than John (John 4:1–3).
Only Mark gives the words of Jesus’ preaching here: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand.” Matthew gives a shorter summary a few verses later (Matthew 4:17).
Luke alone says Jesus returned “in the power of the Spirit” and taught in the synagogues, glorified by all.
John alone mentions the stay in Samaria, the saying about a prophet’s own country, and the Galileans who had seen His works at the feast in Jerusalem.

fit.question: Matthew and Mark say Jesus went to Galilee after John was put in prison. But John says that while Jesus was baptizing in Judea, John “had not yet been thrown into prison” (John 3:24), and that Jesus left Judea because of the Pharisees. Do the accounts clash?

points.label: John fills in earlier months
points.text: Matthew, Mark and Luke begin Jesus’ public work in Galilee after John’s arrest. John alone tells of the months before it, when both men were baptizing. His note in John 3:24 places those months before the arrest, so they fit before the point where the other Gospels begin.

points.label: Two reasons, one journey
points.text: John’s arrest was the signal to go to Galilee, where Jesus took up John’s call to repent. The Pharisees’ growing attention was the reason to leave Judea (John 4:1–3). McGarvey notes that one journey can have both causes, and each writer names the one that serves his account.

fit.note: John’s Gospel supplies months the other writers pass over. The pieces fit together without strain.
fit.short: John tells of months before the Baptist’s arrest; the others begin after it. Both reasons, the arrest and the Pharisees, shaped one journey.

scene.label: Herod’s Galilee
scene.text: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea. He had locked John up for rebuking his marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife (Luke 3:19–20). Going to Galilee meant preaching under the nose of the ruler who had just silenced John.

scene.label: Galilee
scene.text: Galilee was a fertile, crowded region of farming villages and fishing towns around the lake. Its people were Jews, but Jerusalem’s leaders looked down on it (John 7:52), and a Galilean’s speech gave him away (Mark 14:70).

scene.label: The kingdom of God
scene.text: Israel’s prophets had promised a day when God would reign openly, set things right and rescue His people (Daniel 2:44; Isaiah 52:7). Jews in Jesus’ day longed for that kingdom. Jesus announced that its time had come.

scene.label: A prophet’s own country
scene.text: Jesus used this saying more than once (Luke 4:24; Mark 6:4). In John 4:44 it is not clear which place is meant: Judea, where He was born and where the leaders were growing wary; Galilee as a whole; or His hometown of Nazareth. Each reading has able defenders.

witnesses.matthew: Ties Jesus’ move to John’s arrest, then shows Him settling in Capernaum to fulfill Isaiah’s promise of a great light for “Galilee of the Gentiles” (Matthew 4:13–16). For Matthew, the King’s public work begins where the prophet said the light would dawn.
witnesses.mark: Gives Jesus’ first preaching in His own words: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom is at hand, repent and believe. Mark calls it the gospel of the kingdom of God, echoing the first line of his book, “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ” (Mark 1:1).
witnesses.luke: Stresses that Jesus came “in the power of the Spirit,” the same Spirit who came on Him at His baptism and led Him in the wilderness (Luke 4:1). Luke’s summary of synagogue teaching sets up the very next scene, in the synagogue at Nazareth.
witnesses.john: Explains why Galilee was ready to welcome Him: many Galileans had seen His signs at the Passover in Jerusalem (John 2:23). John also records Jesus’ saying about a prophet’s honor, and in his next scene Jesus presses a Galilean father on faith that rests on signs (John 4:48).

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the One in whom God’s promised time arrives. John announced that the kingdom was near; Jesus brings it, with the Spirit’s power resting on Him.
seeing.living: Jesus’ first public call in Mark has two parts: repent, and believe the good news. The kingdom did not wait for calmer days; it came in the very season John was locked up. Answer His call in the circumstances you are actually in.
seeing.ponder: What are you waiting for before you answer Jesus’ call to repent and believe, when He says the time is already fulfilled?

preaching.big_idea: When John’s voice was silenced, Jesus announced that God’s time had come.
outline: A dark moment: John in prison (14a)
Good news: the gospel of the kingdom (14b)
A fulfilled time: the kingdom at hand (15a)
A personal call: repent and believe (15b)
preaching.watch_for: Mark’s summary has two statements and two commands. The statements say what God has done: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom is at hand. The commands say how to respond. God’s action comes before the call.
